Learn how to strengthen your project planning and execution with proven strategies and best practices. This course explores advanced techniques in resource management, stakeholder engagement, and avoiding common project pitfalls. Through hands-on activities and real-world examples, you'll gain practical tools to guide complex projects to success. The learning objectives for this course include: 1) develop and implement effective project management plans; 2) optimize resource allocation and balance project priorities; 3) understand and avoid common project risks and pitfalls; 4) utilize KPIs, OKRs, and EVM to monitor project performance and drive continuous improvement.

As projects grow in complexity, mastering advanced Agile techniques becomes essential. This course builds on your foundational knowledge by exploring how to apply Agile across multiple teams, enhance collaboration, and improve sprint performance. You'll strengthen stakeholder engagement strategies, streamline backlog refinement, and use Agile metrics to support continuous improvement. The learning objectives for this course include: 1) apply strategies for scaling Agile in complex project environments; 2) improve backlog refinement and sprint planning for team effectiveness; 3) use Agile metrics and reporting.

Uncertainty is a part of every project and the ability to manage risk effectively can make the difference between success and failure. This course provides students with practical strategies for identifying and responding to project risks, along with an understanding of how risk management relates to both scope and resource management. You'll learn risk fundamentals, how to plan for and mitigate risk, how to communicate risk effectively to stakeholders, and the important ways risk management integrates will all elements of project planning. The learning objectives for this course include: 1) identify and categorize potential project risks; 2) develop structured risk management and communication plans; 3) implement stakeholder communication strategies for risk management; and 4) understand how risk management integrates with scope and resource management.

Strengthen your leadership skills and learn how to inspire high-performing teams by mastering strategies for team dynamics, conflict resolution, and clear communication. In this hands-on course, you'll explore a variety of leadership styles, practice negotiation techniques, and build executive presence through presentation exercises and role-play simulations. Walk away with practical tools to lead confidently and engage stakeholders for stronger project outcomes. The learning objectives for this course include: 1) develop leadership styles that enhance project team performance; 2) apply communication strategies to engage diverse stakeholder groups; 3) implement conflict resolution and negotiation techniques; 4) Strengthen emotional intelligence and active listening skills for better team dynamics.

Discover how to use AI to work smarter across every phase of your project. Learn to track performance in real time, automate reporting, and detect risks before they escalate. This course offers hands-on experience with AI-driven project management tools designed to streamline decision-making and boost outcomes. You'll also explore key ethical considerations around data use, bias, and transparency in AI-powered workflows, and stay ahead of the curve with an AI Trends Update that highlights the latest innovations shaping the future of project work. The learning objectives for this course include: 1) identify trends and risks in using AI for project management; 2) understand AI's application for project quality management; 3) use AI-powered tools to monitor project performance and automate project reporting; 4) implement AI-based evaluation frameworks to improve project closing processes.

An exploration of methods of cutting images in wood and printing them on paper, including black and white multi-block color, rice paper, and mold-made rag papers, press printing, and hand burnishing.  Woods include solid pine, birch ply, mahogany ply, and others.  Insights into the field of printmaking in general.  Emphasis on continuing development of the relief print.  Evaluation based on a portfolio of work plus general energy and involvement.  Students buy a set of Japanese tools (unless they have adequate tools).

Survey of technical methods involved in developing and printing of screen images on paper.  Stencil building methods feature photo film (with photographic, xerox, and drawn imagery) but also include a range of hand-built methods (glue, resist, cut film, paper stencil, etc.).  Insights into the field of printmaking in general.  Students may build their own screens or use furnished screens.  Emphasis on continuing development of individual personal imagery in the context of the screen print.  Evaluation based on a portfolio of work plus general energy and involvement.
The course introduces more advanced techniques to students.  Areas include relief, screenprint, lithography, intaglio and mixed media.
The course introduces more advanced techniques to students.  Areas include relief, screenprint, lithography, intaglio, and mixed media.

Darkroom Film Photography is an introductory in the photography emphasis. This course focuses on basic black-and-white film processing, darkroom printing, and paper development. Students are required to use a 35mm manual camera with adjustable aperture and shutter speeds. If a student does not have a camera, one can be checked out from the photography area. This class focuses on basic camera operations, including shutter speed, aperture, depth-of-field, and film speed (ISO). Students will learn to think and see photographically and incorporate elements of design, framing, composition, and perspective.This course is open to all photography majors and minors and Film & Media Arts majors.

This class is an introduction and exploration into the use of the computers as an art-making tool and as a medium for visual communications. Scanning, image manipulation, and printing have become essential skills for all artists. Students will learn to use digital tools including Adobe Photoshop and illustrator, to make images that are meaningful, creative, and communicate effectively.

Medium & Large Format Photography focuses on advanced camera operations and film and darkroom techniques using medium format and large format 4x5 view cameras. This course introduces more advanced photographic concepts through group discussions, readings, lectures, and individual projects, while continuing to emphasize aesthetic presentation. Additionally, various technical controls are investigated, including water-bath developing, bleaching and toning, archival printing, and zone system.Medium format and large format 4x5 view cameras are available for check-out from the photography area. Various technical controls are investigated, including water-bath developing, bleaching and toning, archival printing. The student is also made aware of historical and critical issues through a reading list and slide presentations. Group discussions are an integral part of this course.

Digital Technology has affected every aspect of the photographic process. Historically, new tools have lead to new forms of expression. Using tools learned in the preceding classes, students will explore visual issues unique to digital photography. Students will develop their personal vision and explore extended possibilities of the medium through a series of projects based on questions about the nature of contemporary photography. This class also explores technologies (such as video and 3D computer modeling ) that are new to contemporary fine arts photography. This class assumes that students are well grounded in technical skills and are prepared to use digital tools to explore aesthetic issues and advanced concepts.

Chemical, physical, and biological properties of synthetic polymer, metal, and ceramic biomaterials.  Relationship between the structure of biomaterials and their interaction with blood, soft, and hard tissue.  Mechanical properties, fabrication, and degradation mechanisms, and performance testing of materials in biomedical use.
Arranged as needed by master's candidates.

This course will review fundamental aspects of pharmacokinetics with an emphasis on understanding concepts for compartmental and non-compartmental modeling, physiologic modeling, and modeling of targeted drug delivery systems. The goal of the course is to understand how these techniques can be used to optimize drug delivery.

Physicochemical fundamentals of dosage form design.  Molecular thermodynamics approach to establishing principles of solutions, structures of liquids and solids, complexation, ion-solvent interactions, and multiple equilibria of organic solutes.  Physicochemical examination of peptides and proteins, and protein structures.  Thermodynamics of nucleic acids: temperature effects, cooperativity, and hybridization equilibria.  Principles of colloid and interfacial sciences applied to pharmaceutical dosage formulations.

Introduction to lipid systems in Pharmaceutics and drug delivery.  Emulsions, micellar and vesicular carriers.  Biorecognition and drug targeting of small molecule, protein, and nucleic acid therapeutics.

Biocompatibility of soluble and insoluble (crosslinked) polymers. Biocompatibility of biomaterials used as implants, blood substitutes, and carriers of bioactive molecules. Biorecognition of synthetic macromolecules on cellular and subcellular levels.  Biodegradability and immunogenicity of biomaterials.
Seminar on personal research or assigned literature surveys.
Conferences, library, and laboratory work as arranged.
Reports from current pharmaceutics and related literature.

This course covers nucleic acid metabolism, including purines and pyrimidines, DNA replication and repair, RNA and protein synthesis, regulation of gene transcription and translation. Topics also include cell structure components, ion channels and receptors, mitosis and meiosis, cell cycle, genetics, pharmacogenomics, recombinant DNA methods, biologics, molecular diagnostic methods, gene editing and gene therapy.

Delivery of pharmaceutical services to community; didactic material and in depth case studies involving patient profiles, compliance, over-the-counter medications, prescription accessories, and patient counseling. Additional work required of PharmD students.

This course will introduce pharmacy students to the legal, ethical, and risk management issues that are foundational in the practice of pharmacy. Course content will focus on statues, regulation, standards of practice, and case law. Students will also develop skills for ethical issue identification, critical reasoning and analysis. These skills will enable students to better integrate core principles of basic and clinical sciences within a balance of legal requirements, ethical rules, public policy, and societal interests.

This course is taught in the second semester of the first professional year as a follow-up to PHARM 5140. In-class discussions and speakers require students to integrate assigned readings with speaker presentations on the many aspects of providing and receiving service and medical care. The course is intended to provide depth on issues relative to diversity, social awareness and civic responsibility, anchored to material from other PharmD courses that discuss the safety, economic, social and political aspects of health care provision from a patient-centered care perspective.

The Pharmacy Practice Skills Lab series will emphasize the practice of foundational patient care skills while integrating knowledge learned in other courses with their practical applications in pharmacy practice. The primary skills emphasized during this longitudinal course include: patient physical assessment, medication history, patient interviews, medication counseling, SBARQ, and SOAP note writing. In PPSLII, the focused skills will include general physical assessment and patient interviewing.

This recitation course will provide active learning sessions in which students in the P1 Spring Semester improve their understanding of the foundational material being taught in the P1 curriculum and begin learning how to apply this foundational knowledge to the practice of pharmacy. Recitations will further facilitate the development of students' professionalism, including professional communication skills, and evidence-based approaches to pharmaceutical care.

The purpose of this seminar series is to foster in P1 students the knowledge, skills, abilities, behaviors, and attitudes necessary to demonstrate self-awareness, leadership, and professionalism throughout their careers. Students will participate in professional development workshops, complete portfolio assignments, and will be required to meet with their assigned mentor(s) each semester.

Basic principles of in-vivo drug kinetics (linear and non-linear); principles of bioavailability/bioequivalence; physiologic determinates of drug onset and duration; concepts of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion; the pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic interface; dosage regimen design; renal and hepatic clearance; using pharmacodynamics to estimate drug half-life and adjust dosages.

This course builds off of Foundations of Drug Information and Drug Literature Evaluation I to introduce principles of biostatistics, pharmacoeconomics, and critical appraisal of the medical literature. These skills form a foundation for evidence-based practice. The second semester will emphasize noninferiority clinical trials, systematic reviews and meta-analysis, and pharmacoeconomic studies.

The Pharmacy Practice Skills Lab series will emphasize the practice of foundational patient care skills while integrating knowledge learned in other courses with their practical applications in pharmacy practice. The primary skills emphasized during this longitudinal course include: patient physical assessment, medication history, patient interviews, medication counseling, SBARQ, and SOAP note writing. In PPSLIV, the focused skills will include complete medication review and musculoskeletal/neurological physical assessment.

Recitation will utilize active, team-based instructional methodologies that challenges students to integrate students to integrate knowledge and skills taught across the courses in the Spring of the P2 year. All methods will engage students in active learning and empower students in developing foundational problem solving, effective communication, critical-thinking analysis and reasoning, and professional skills development. These methods are specifically designed to stimulate professional maturity and development. These methods are specifically designed to stimulate professional maturity and development. Small group discussions will be facilitated by basic science faculty, post docs and residents/fellows.

Integrated Pharmacotherapeutics II is divided into three modules: 1) Central Nervous System, 2) Pulmonary, and 3) Infectious Disease. In each of these modules, the relevant pathophysiology, medicinal chemistry, pharmacology, toxicology and therapeutics will be presented in an integrated way, having the overall objectives of understanding current pharmacotherapeutic approaches, and knowing the basic science underpinnings of those approaches, for management of important disease conditions.

This interdisciplinary course is designed to prepare students for deliberately working together to improve the safety and quality of the health care utilizing telemedicine technology in rural communities. Through simulation-based patient care management scenarios, health profession students are provided the opportunity to engage in interactive learning with other disciplines using this technology. Complex patient care management simulation form the basis for these interprofessional experiences designed to teach the principles of team-based communication, patient-centered care for patients with multiple chronic illness.

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines Interprofessional education (IPE) as an experience that “occurs when students from two or more professions learn about, from, and with each other” (WHO, 2010). The goal of interprofessional education is to increase knowledge of the roles and responsibilities of other health care professions, and to improve communication and collaboration among disciplines in future work settings to optimize patient care (Institute of Medicine, 2011). The purpose of this interprofessional education course is to introduce students in health professional training programs at the University of Utah to the roles and responsibilities of other health care professions at an early stage of their training.

This interprofessional education course prepares students to disclose medical errors as a health professional team. Teams of students from various health professions including pharmacy, medicine, nursing, physicians assistant, and others participate in an in-person simulation to disclose a medication error in a hospital setting that could result in serious harm or death of the patient. Students learn the basic principles of effective error disclosure in an authentic scenario where they play the role of their profession on a health care team.

The purpose of this seminar series is to foster in P2 students the knowledge, skills, abilities, behaviors, and attitudes necessary to demonstrate self-awareness, leadership, and professionalism throughout their careers. Students will participate in professional development workshops, complete portfolio assignments, and will be required to meet with their assigned mentor(s) each semester.

This course examines advanced pharmacy practice in several settings including community practice, primary care, acute care, critical care, managed care, transitions of care and specialty pharmacy. Case studies focus on patients with multiple interlocking disease states, using a team-based learning approach.

This course examines the impact of present and proposed public policy on the US health care system. In-class discussions will emphasize the complexity of our health care system; the myriad of issues it faces; as well as potential public policy solutions to these issues. In addition, an active learning approach will be used to empower students to communicate about health policy issues to other stakeholders in the systems including individuals, patients, health care professionals and decision-makers.

The Pharmacy Practice Skills Lab series will emphasize the practice of foundational patient care skills while integrating knowledge learned in other courses with their practical applications in pharmacy practice. The primary skills emphasized during this longitudinal course include: patient physical assessment, medication history, patient interviews, medication counseling, SBARQ, and SOAP note writing. In PPSLIV, the focused skills will include complete medication review and musculoskeletal/neurological physical assessment.
Application of pharmacy management to various settings that represent professional pharmacy practice through video based virtual scenarios.

From a broad perspective, all healthcare professions need effective leadership, and in turn effective advocacy, to deal with the numerous issues facing the health care system. This two credit elective is offered to provide leadership and political advocacy development for student pharmacists and PhD students in the College of Pharmacy who desire to become leaders in the profession. Students will examine leadership as they explore current health care issues and gain direct experience in the advocacy process and community action. To meet these needs, the goals of this course are to strengthen the leadership ability of students and to enhance their potential for future leadership and advocacy roles within their profession and in the community.
Fundamental principles of production, control, distribution, and use of radiopharmaceuticals.

This course will allow the student to gain in-depth practical knowledge of oncologic disease states, chemotherapy management, and patient perspective via active learning activities and interaction with local expert facilitators.

This course will allow the student to gain in-depth practical knowledge of thrombosis disease states, anti-thrombotic therapy management, and patient perspectives via active learning activities and interaction with thrombosis experts.

The purpose of this course is to provide students with fundamentals of solid organ transplantation. This course will begin with an overview of transplantation, the history of transplantation, and an immunology review. Post-transplant management of kidney, pancreas, liver, heart, and lung transplants will be discussed. Students will learn about the various phases of immunosuppression across different organ transplants. Finally, students will also have the opportunity to learn about commonly encountered infectious diseases in immunosuppressed patients.

The course provides students with an interdisciplinary (e.g., medicine, nursing, pharmacy, and ethics) discourse on the provision of pain and symptom control for patients with life limiting disease. The course will focus on attitudes, knowledge, and skills for different providers and on interdisciplinary teaching to navigate the complexities of care required by people facing the end-of-life transition.

The primary purpose of this online elective is to provide students tools and the experience needed to provide outreach education programs to a variety of audiences. It is our hope that after graduation, students will continue to provide poison prevention education in the community in which they practice. Utah Poison Control Center’s outreach education efforts are directed to people of all ages including parents of children under six years of age, pre-school students, and older adults. Outreach efforts include minority groups and other disadvantaged populations. Examples of outreach include tabling and presentations at Safe Kids fairs, senior centers, schools, and other community events.

This course introduces students to regulatory principles (regulatory affairs, regulatory sciences), and intellectual property.  This content is anticipated as useful to those considering a career in pharmaceutical or biotechnology industry, academia, or government.  This course will primarily focus on US laws and regulations, (FDA, PHS, USPTO); however, as pharmaceutical and biological therapies are a multi-national, global industry, there will be a brief introduction to international regulatory affairs (Health Canada, European Medicines Agency [EMA], PMDA [Japan]) and international intellectual property (Paris Convention, and WIPO).

An elective course designed to increase the depth and breadth of infectious diseases diagnostics and effective medication use. The course will highlight the specialty of infectious diseases through a case-based approach. Students will be applying principles learned in their training to previously unknown infections. Students will be challenged to evaluate cases presented in progress notes and lab findings, identify resources to address best treatment of these patients, and communicate their assessment and propose a plan for these patients.

Students will meet to discuss components of their projects, receive feedback from peers and faculty, and participate in small group work.

PharmD graduate students must register for PHARM 7950 for the semester in which they participate in a cooperative work experience for curricular practical training (CPT), on-the-job cooperative education. Designed exclusively for international students, this course is required for the international student who wishes to participate in curricular practical training through an off-campus internship. Students must enroll in this class each semester that they work off-campus. Students will submit detailed course objectives, a final paper describing what was learned in this job, and an updated resume including the internship.

This course is designed to provide basic didactic information in the underlying concepts of pharmacology for the beginning graduate student. The primary emphasis of the course is to provide new graduate students in the Department of Pharmacology and Toxicology, or other graduate students in the biomedical sciences (Neuroscience, Biological Chemistry, or Molecular Biology programs) with fundamental knowledge about pharmacology and drug treatment. It is anticipated that students who complete this course would be able to apply these fundamental concepts to more advanced curricula and research endeavors in the disciplines of pharmacology and toxicology.

General principles, testing procedures, toxic responses, and target organ toxicities. This course is designed to familiarize students with adverse effects that chemicals may produce based on the dose, exposure and hazard of those chemicals. There will be a focus on mechanisms of toxicity in different organ systems (Neurotoxicology, cardiovascular, lungs, skin and kidney toxicology) that are relevant based on common exposure. The course will also cover environmental toxicology, toxic effects of pesticides, and natural products.

An on-line introductory course exploring the foundations of the profession of Physical Therapy, including: a) roles and responsibilities of physical therapists; b) patient/client management; c) The American Physical Therapy Association; d) legal and ethical PT practice perspectives; e) current PT practice issues; f) basic principles of current practice standards for common musculoskeletal, neuromuscular, cardiopulmonary, integumentary, pediatric, and geriatric conditions.  This course is appropriate for pre-physical therapy students and those wishing to learn more about the profession in general.

This course is appropriate for pre-physical therapy students and those wishing to learn more about the profession in general.

Basic principles and interpretation of diagnostic imaging modalities as they apply to physical therapy are covered in this course. The course emphasizes plain film radiography, including basic physics of the imaging technique, viewing and interpreting films, radiographic anatomy, and clinical correlation with patient cases. Other imaging modalities including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), scintigraphy (bone scan), and contrast films will also be included. Following introductory material the course will be taught from a regional perspective.

Physical therapists traditionally deliver care within a third party payor reimbursement model.  However, contemporary physical therapy practice has expanded to include alternate models of delivery of care, including but not limited to the PT as primary care provider and as coordinator of primary and secondary prevention programs.  This course provides the student with an opportunity to present, analyze and integrate case studies of physical therapy practice as the provider for alternate models of care.  Case studies are drawn from patients with simple to complex problems in the general medicine, cardiopulmonary, musculoskeletal, integumentary, and neuromuscular systems, and who present to the physical therapist as a first point of contact for health care.  Emphasis is placed on the physical therapist's role, responsibilities, and risks when practicing as an entry point into the health care system and when participating in preventative programs.  Additional emphasis will be on critiquing and designing fitness and wellness programs for populations with special needs.  Programs will focus on those for employee fitness, diabetes, arthritis, osteoporosis, obesity and the elderly.  Students will participate in and evaluate group treatments and recreational exercise.

Students will also have an opportunity to work with various allied health providers such as physical therapist to better understand the role of these individuals in the rehabilitation process. Understanding the link between population health and specialty/sub-specialty medical care is a critical component aspect of public health.  This course uses principles of surgical care in the developing world to illustrate the integration of this type of medical practice and public health.  The instructors of this course bring together expertise in the fields of surgery and public health to provide a rich educational experience that focuses on the delicate balance of individual- and population-level care.

The practice of surgery is rarely considered a public health issue in the United States. however, surgical issues, including trauma and emergency care are gaining recognition as major components of public health on par with infectious diseases, both in the developed and in the developing world. this course uses principles of medical care in the developing world to illustrate the integration of surgery as a component of public health. The instructors of this course bring together expertise in the fields of surgery and public health to provide a rich educational experience that focuses on the delicate balance of individual and population-levels of care. This course will form the foundation for further problem-based learning coursework.

Students will write an introduction for a currently in-progress or planned paper. Other assignments will include a scientific poster and a commentary in response to a recently published article. This course provides in-depth training in causal methods focused on causality claims in public health and the current study design and analytical methods that strengthen such claims. This includes the counterfactual/potential outcomes framework, causal estimands, mathematical conditions under which associational measures of effect equal causal measures, paths of confounding and selection bias, and time-dependent confounding. It includes experimental versus observational study designs and natural experiments. Analytical methods include propensity score models, inverse probability of treatment weighting, g-computation, g-estimation and associated techniques from econometrics. Selected advanced topics will be covered, such as extensions of analytic techniques to effect modification, mediation analysis, targeted learning, clustered data, and dynamic treatment regimes.

Utah Opera's preview class will provide insights into the story and the music, as well as the production history of Verdi's "La traviata." We will also present fascinating information about Utah Opera's production and its cast. Interested class members can linger after the hour-long class session to observe a rehearsal on-site. Presented through University of Utah Osher Lifelong Learning Institute by Opera Education Manager Kevin Nakatani and Principal Coach Deborah Rober. It's a timeless tale of love, sacrifice, and heartbreak. Verdi's "La traviata" takes you deep into the world of Violetta, a glamorous Parisian courtesan who falls for the charming Alfredo. Their passionate romance is tragically challenged by social expectations and personal sacrifice, proving that not all love stories have a happy ending--but they're unforgettable stories all the same. "La traviata" has everything opera lovers crave--fiery emotions, gorgeous arias, and a plot that pulls at your heartstrings.

This course will examine the odd, unusual, and unique libraries throughout the world, as well as world famous libraries. Libraries are rich with exciting and surprising stories! This class will "check them out."

There's no shortage of forgotten women in history: women who spoke when they were told to be silent, stayed when they were told to leave, and who never wavered in forging change. In every historical period, there have been women whose stories have been ignored or simply lost to time. In this course, we will look at some of those women in the areas of science and technology, women in war, political change-makers, athletes, and women in the arts. We will make connections between brave and innovative women in history and modern-day champions, Nobel Prize winners, and those who changed the course of human achievement. Standing on the shoulders of giants, these new generations of women go on to create great innovations and initiate change that has had, and will continue to have, global impacts.

John Wecker served three tours in Afghanistan as a Foreign Service Officer with the U.S. Department of State between 2008 and 2019. While there, he was an advisor to Afghanistan's only female governor in Bamiyan, led rule of law programming in Mazar-e- Sharif, and was the political advisor to the Commander of the Joint Special Forces, Afghanistan at Bagram. During this lecture presentation, John will describe his unique experiences from that time, illustrate his lecture with his extensive photo collection, and share his thoughts on what became America's longest running war.

The Muslim population in Russia, while a relatively small percentage (10-15%) of the overall populace, still represents a significant number (15-20 million people). Furthermore, this population is concentrated in two key regions where Muslims are the majority (North Caucasus and Tatarstan/Bashkortostan), making them important players in Russian politics, both domestically and internationally. This course will delve into these Muslim-majority areas, exploring their historical conversion to Islam, the demographic, social, and cultural distinctions between Muslim and non-Muslim Russians, and the internal differences between the two Muslim-majority regions themselves.

Class members will learn beginning techniques such as easy chords, strum patterns, and exercises. This will result in being able to play easy songs on the ukulele in traditional and contemporary music styles, such as pop, folk, country, and more!

Taking the time to listen to our inner voice can help guide us to make important decisions, boost our creativity, consider new opportunities, and help us clarify our values and purpose. We all have the ability to listen to our inner voice, but it often gets crowded out by our outer life and we rarely take the time to pause, reflect, and trust what it might be telling us. Writing can help! Writing can provide insight and change our perspective. By putting pen to paper, we turn off our inner critic, allowing us to make sense of our thoughts without edits or judgement. Through writing we can clear out the noise, delve deeper, and reveal the wisdom of our inner voice. In a relaxed and safe environment, we will explore the wisdom of our inner voice through short readings, writing prompts, and writing-related discussions. All writing levels are welcome. No writing experience is necessary.

You joined Osher and paid your membership dues for a year of fun. Now what? This single-session free class will welcome new members, provide a "meet and greet" opportunity to socialize a bit with others new to Osher, and show you the ropes of how to get involved. We will cover the material in our Member Handbook, letting you know how you can get the most out of your membership benefits...everything from where to get your U of U student ID card, to where to use it for discounts, to the many campus amenities available to Continuing Education students. Our program becomes stronger with each new member!

Did you ever wonder about how the Osher program operates behind the scenes? This single-session free class will introduce you to the magic of how Osher staff and volunteers recruit instructors, organize classes, and create four fascinating six-week terms each year. We will outline duties performed by the esteemed Osher Curriculum Committee. Our founder, Bernard Osher, intended his Osher Lifelong Learning Institutes to be member-driven and volunteer-led within a community of peers, ages 50 and better. Every single member, instructor, and volunteer brings their wealth of life experiences and knowledge to the classroom, building a very special community of curious adults who value education and class discussions highly. Come learn how it's done, share your ideas, and maybe even think about teaching a course yourself for your fellow Osher members.

If you are an instructor who is teaching for Osher in an upcoming term, or if you are considering submitting a proposal to teach a course, this orientation class is for you! In this orientation, Osher staff will cover all the ins and outs of running an Osher class. We will inform you of all policies and procedures for in-person and Zoom classes, including creating syllabi, sending and printing handouts, getting your enrollment numbers and class rosters, taking attendance, technology help in the classroom or on Zoom, class cancellations, scheduling makeup classes, and more. We will let you know how to claim perks available to you as an associate instructor at the University of Utah. Welcome aboard!

Do you love Osher and want to give back to this wonderful program by serving as a volunteer? We would love to have you! We are currently seeking volunteers to serve as Osher Ambassadors to help greet and direct people at our annual open house at Red Butte Garden in August, annual member luncheon at Little America Hotel in December, and our Spring Fling held on campus in early March. Osher Ambassadors will help staff with various tasks at these big events and also help host free special events throughout the year, attending as an Osher member who gathers the group at the designated meeting spot, takes roll, and communicates with staff afterwards. During our four terms, Osher Ambassadors can also help instructors by taking roll in classes and reading announcements each week before class begins, as well as directing members to our complimentary coffee and tea service and their classrooms during the "first week of school" when Osher members are trying to find the way to their new class. This is a low effort but high impact and fun way to get involved. You can sign up to help at as many or as few events or classes as your schedule allows. Join us to learn more about this opportunity in a fun, free class session.

Silent film is composed of silence, black and white imagery, the speeding up of action in the films shown at a faster rate than they are shot, the reliance on the audience as an unwitting collaborator in storytelling, and the live musical accompaniment. All of these make up the sound of silents, and it is a language all its own. Create your own dialogue based on the visual cues from the screen and learn how the language of silence is silent film's greatest asset.

"If you were the kind of kid that always asked "Why?" - this is your class. What is reality? Scientists have labeled their search for reality as the "Theory of Everything." Using physics and chemistry, the solution was straight forward until they encountered "Quantum Theory", then things became "uncertain". However, recent research (Nobel prize 2022) has introduced a revolutionary idea for the ultimate blueprint of the universe from atoms to galaxies. We will study how this approach may also answer the question, "What is consciousness"? We will connect the "very big and very small" objects in the universe (including Big Bang, dark matter, and the Standard Model) with the latest theories of space and time (including relativity & quantum theory). These sessions will establish an understanding of why science has been so successful in establishing technologies (e.g. The World of Chemistry and the Age of Information) and introduce new theories that are revolutionizing the future of science. After being confident about a perspective of reality, we will conclude by looking at how the future of science may affect our personal reality."

This is the story of the Theater of the Mind. Radio was the central medium of news and entertainment in America until television nearly killed it. But rock 'n' roll came along and the medium was reborn, first as Top 40 radio. Later, as the audience migrated from the AM to the FM dial, underground or freeform radio dominated the airwaves and captured the imagination of popular culture. It changed the music business permanently and birthed the Classic Era of Rock. We listen to the music and look at where it came from, how it happened, and what became of it.

Rich with themes about aging and life, the 2025 bestselling novel, The Correspondent, by Virginia Evans, will be the jumping off point for our class. Aging, grief, relationships, resilience, forgiveness, and hope are among the many topics woven throughout The Correspondent we will explore in our writing. Since the story is told exclusively through letters and correspondence, we'll also write letters of our own. Please read The Correspondent before the first class. All writing levels are welcome!

Frederick Douglass was a visionary--a prophet who could see a better future that lay just beyond reach. His talents were nothing short of extraordinary, and he put his exceptional gifts to use in the service of freedom, driving American slavery into the grave. In this talk, we'll explore this many-sided man's life, family, and career, and consider his impact upon our modern struggle to advance the cause of Black freedom in the United States.

Franklin's genius is a puzzle. Here is a man with only two years of proper schooling who later received honorary degrees from Harvard, Yale, Oxford, and St. Andrews as well as the eighteenth-century equivalent of a Nobel Prize for Physics. In this talk University of Maryland historian Richard Bell will examine many of Franklin's ideas to make life simpler, cheaper, and easier for himself and everyone else. It turns out that those ideas encompassed not only natural science and engineering, but also all sorts of public works, civic improvements, political trail-blazing, and fresh, new business ideas.

Benedict Arnold is the most famous turncoat in American history. He was a skilled officer in George Washington's Continental Army who began secretly communicating with British intelligence agents, giving them insider information, and dramatically defecting to their side in return for a mountain of cash. Historian Richard Bell reconstructs the life and times of Benedict Arnold, the reasons for this treason, and the larger problems of betrayal and desertion that dogged the Continental Army throughout the war.

This course will provide an overview of the Clean Water Act, one of the United States's foundational federal environmental laws. Beginning with background on the science of water pollution and history of water quality regulation, the course will introduce students to the factors that shaped the current contours of the law. This course introduces and examines the major provisions of the Clean Water Act, including the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES), Section 404 dredge-and-fill permitting, and establishment of water quality standards and the Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) program. In addition to examining the Act's individual provisions, we will discuss ongoing legal developments, assess the impacts of the law, and engage with critiques of the Clean Water Act's shortcomings.

Thanks to the efforts by actively engaged artists, art historians, scholars, and curators around the world, more women artists are being written about, their works put on display, and their art sold for greater amounts. In this class, we will explore women whose work helped shape the course of art history from the 19th to the 20th centuries.

In this class we will stroll (virtually) through a history of Utah architecture from the earliest to the present. Along the way, we will stop to examine the economic, material, sociocultural, environmental, technological, and other factors that have influenced the evolution of how buildings in Utah have looked. We will ponder intriguing questions like: What prompted the Ancient Puebloans to build cliff dwellings? Why is Thomas Jefferson lurking in Utah's civic buildings? How did the design of churches change in the 20th century (or not)--and why? No expertise or experience in architecture required. Just an interest in what we see around us.

In October of 1492 Christopher Columbus 'discovered' the Americas. He failed to mention that North America was populated by at least ten million Native Americans, who arrived on the continent at least 20,000 years ago. Initially they were hunters and gatherers, but over time, resources were depleted and with the arrival of corn and squash at about 1500 BCE, agriculture developed. This was the birth of the Anasazi culture, the most sophisticated culture in North America for over a thousand years. There are over 150,000 archeological sites in San Juan County alone. Many of these sites are beautifully preserved today in cliff dwellings. This is the focus of the course. We will explore these sites and learn much of the Anasazi Culture in Utah.

Each class will start with an overview of a few important aspects of the craft of poetry, followed by time for each participant to practice writing. We will have an opportunity to share, optionally, what we have started. Some topics we will cover include meter, metaphors/similes, form poems, free verse, line endings, and finding an engaging title. As to prior background in writing poetry, this is not required. However, it is expected that participants are currently reading poetry and are inspired to set aside time to write their own poems. Participants should bring something to write on (e.g., a notebook) and write with (e.g., a pen).

What is love? Krishnamurti said that if someone says they understand love, then they probably don't. Yet we all seem to know that love gives our lives meaning and purpose. In this course, we will explore the mysteries of love from a variety of perspectives, including the ecological, biological, psychological, philosophical, social, and spiritual. As in all of Dr. Dave's classes, we will learn through a skillful mix of class dialogues and presentations. Come join us!

This course explores the intersection of psychedelics and human development through historical, scientific, psychological, and spiritual lenses. Class members will examine the cultural roots and modern resurgence of psychedelic substances, learn about their therapeutic uses, and engage with cutting-edge research on their potential to address mental health challenges. Emphasis will be placed on the biopsychosocial-spiritual model of healing, offering a holistic framework for understanding transformation and integration. By the end of the course, class members will have a deeper understanding of how psychedelics can influence identity, healing, and growth--both individually and collectively.

This class will explore the history, geography, culture, and ongoing evolution of Salt Lake City. We will look at the city's founding, growth, and modern development. Topics will include: 1) building Salt Lake City, its layout, architecture, and community planning; 2) the area's industry and its growth; 3) transportation and growth from the wagon trains to TRAX; 4) the surrounding canyons and how they helped shape the valley; and 5) the lost stories of Salt Lake City and its lost neighborhoods. We will compare aspects of Salt Lake City from the past to the present.

David McCullough, "America's Historian," wrote numerous award-winning books. This course is designed to "whet your appetite" for reading his books. We will be exploring the historical significance of each book including, where it fits on the historical timeline, the location, economics, politics, and societal norms at the time of the events covered in each book. We will also be looking at the author himself, his life, and his other contributions to history.

This course introduces you to the basics of Zentangle, then takes you beyond to create more challenging work. Zentangle is a method of meditative art making using "tangles," or structured patterns using "elemental" strokes: dots, lines, curves, and orbs. Each creation is personal and allows you to relax, increase hand-eye coordination, and connect with others in a creative, positive, online atmosphere. No previous art experience or skill is required. The amazing part comes at the end when all of the work is viewed together in a class "mosaic." Come be a part of making beautiful things together.

The AARP Smart Driver Course is the nation's first and largest 4-hour refresher course designed specifically for older drivers. The goal is for you to become an even safer driver through this program and our additional resources. This course will review driving skills and techniques, as well as strategies and tips to help you adjust to normal age-related changes that may affect your driving ability. As an added bonus, graduates could receive a discount on their auto insurance. Plus it's fun and enjoyable!

Join us for six weeks of creative writing workshops focusing on poetry and prose. Learn about different types of poems such as sonnets and villanelles. Spend time working on your own pieces in class, and share your work with others each week.

This two-part workshop is a study of Korean freestyle painting. Class members will learn a variety of painting skills, using careful and precise brush strokes to control the ink paint. Session one will be bamboo and chrysanthemum. Session two will be orchid and plum tree. We will paint for three hours with a short break in the middle of the session. We will have an enjoyable time creating with this fascinating medium. Korean ink painting is one of the most meditative and fun ways to experience a cultural exchange.

Qigong is a mind-body-spirit practice that improves one's mental and physical health by integrating posture, movement, breathing technique, self-massage, sound, and focused intent. Qigong does not require any skill level or experience. No equipment is needed. Wear comfortable clothes and shoes and learn simple energy practices to release stress, calm your mind and improve your health.

Joseph Campbell was one of the great intellectual voices of the twentieth century. He taught us about how the stories we tell come to define us. Mythology is not make believe; it is the glue that binds cultures together. This course will explore these stories, and Campbell's unique ability to bring them to life. Each week, we will examine a different culture's mythology, and using slide illustrated lectures, readings, and open discussion, gain a better understanding of how the stories we tell shape the world we live within.

Join us for a six week course that breaks down the history of World War Two in both Europe and the Pacific. Taught in tandem by two historians, this class breaks down World War Two by year looking at what is happening simultaneously in both the European and Pacific theatres. Each week, class will be split into two 45 minute segments which will cover what was happening in each arena during a certain year.

Flapper fashion wasn't just popular in the United States, instead it represented a larger phenomenon of women stepping out of and redefining traditional roles to live and thrive in a rapidly modernizing world. In Asia the "Modern Girl" stepped out into a complex society, trying to find a place between tradition, nationalism, colonialism, and consumerism. In this single-session class we will discuss how colonization and modernization created a unique opportunity for women to seek out higher education, involve themselves in work, and adapt traditional fashions to become the iconic figures we remember today.

According to Chinese Calendar and astrology, the Year of the Fire Horse will begin February 17th, 2026 in line with the Chinese New Year. On this day, join us for the Lunar New Year "forecast" from the perspective of Chinese medicine and astrology. In this 1-hour talk, we will explore the basics of the Lunar Calendar and the Chinese Astrology, learn the energetic manifestations of the Fire Horse, and see what the year of the Horse may have in store for us.

Art, artifacts, and family heirlooms are important to our lives and history. In this course we will discuss how best to protect, clean, and when to ask for help to conserve those pieces of art that are important to us.

Air pollution is considered the most important environmental health threat globally, causing and exacerbating several diseases. Recent estimates by the World Health Organization attribute approximately eight million premature deaths per year to air pollution in 2021, amounting to 8% of the global health burden. In this course we will introduce air pollution principles, as well as discuss measurement techniques and our unique challenges faced in Utah. We will study the associated health effects and economic costs, and present policy and planning efforts to improve conditions.

This is an ongoing art history course from Gardner's Art through the Ages. This semester we will look at Early Medieval art and architecture, the Carolingian Renaissance of Charlemagne, along with the introduction of the importance of illuminated manuscripts. We will also include the beautiful castles of the Romanesque period and the secular, luxury arts: tapestries, relics, and decorated books. Finally we will consider the Gothic cathedrals like Chartres and Notre Dame with their fabulous architecture, sculptural designs, and their symbolic stained-glass windows. This section will also include an in-depth presentation on Notre Dame's history, the recent fire, and the rebuilding.

Learn advanced techniques for mastering the music: performing techniques, dynamics, and how to study more advanced pieces with advanced right hand left hand techniques. We will also discuss how to manage our nerves when performing in class and in public.

Learn how to create visually stunning digital stories, travelogues, and more using ArcGIS StoryMaps! ArcGIS StoryMaps is a web-based tool you can use to create interactive narrative stories that combine text, images, data, maps, and more. We'll explore the main features of the platform, learn how the platform can be used in both professional and personal settings, and see how the platform may be used to create engaging online exhibits. This one-day introduction course will inspire you to get started with your own creative project!

You probably know that Christmas was originally a pagan holiday--but what about Easter or Halloween? Are there other holidays with pagan roots? This course explores the origins and evolution of European religious practices that are still celebrated today. We'll familiarize ourselves with the aspects of medieval paganism and how people understood their relationship with nature, spirits, and deities through various rituals and ceremonies. Through a historical lens, we'll trace the impact of Christianity on European pagans like Vikings, Celts, and other pre-Christian groups, and how their cultures evolved, merged with, or were replaced by Christianity. By examining these rituals and their transformations, we can better understand our European ancestors and how their beliefs shaped--and continue to influence--our modern world.

Learn more tips and tricks using Drive and Maps. Become more organized using folders and files for travel, business, family, social activities, and much more. Week one: Focus on Drive Docs, Sheets, & Forms. Week two: Review Maps Navigation, Lists, and Map building, sharing with friends and family. Expand your knowledge and confidence using these Apps through demos and hands-on activities. Bring your laptop and/or tablet to class. Please remember to bring charging cables. Let's have fun while learning!

This is a single-session, 90-minute PowerPoint presentation on selected artists and illustrators who experienced the American Civil War and then depicted what they had witnessed. Included in the presentation are representative paintings and drawings of people such as Winslow Homer and Alfred Waud, a brief description of the works shown in the class, a short biographical sketch of each person mentioned, and information about important magazines or institutions that published or displayed Civil War art and illustrations. Given the importance of and interest in the Civil War, visual representations of the conflict add a significant dimension to the constantly growing body of knowledge which reflect an American war that has been described as not only a watermark period in the history of the United States, but the nation's first modern war.

Nuclear Energy is coming to Utah. Learn about its benefits and risks. Learn about its beginnings, radiation hazards, nuclear accidents that have occurred, its future, safety measures, and possible solutions for nuclear waste disposal. At least half of this class will discuss present and future nuclear power plant designs, including small modular nuclear plants and the TerraPower plant design presently being built in Kemmerer, Wyoming, as well as nuclear waste disposal.

From desert canyons to alpine forests, quiet trails to sweeping vistas, the natural world leaves a lasting imprint on our lives. This course invites participants to virtually reconnect with the outdoor experiences that shaped who they are. Whether from a childhood camping trip, a long-remembered adventure, or a single transformative moment in nature. Through guided writing prompts, gentle craft lessons, and supportive discussion, you'll learn how to turn your memories of the outdoors into meaningful, well-crafted stories. We will explore how place influences identity, how sensory detail can bring a landscape to life, and how reflection gives depth and purpose to personal narratives. No prior writing experience is needed. Bring your curiosity, love of nature, and a desire to preserve the memories that matter most. By the end of the course, you'll have a small collection of nature-based memoir pieces and a deeper appreciation for the landscapes that have shaped your life.

This is an exercise course that will involve some lecture and doing the actual exercises. It is specifically for the 50 plus population and will cover all the necessary physical movements for aging well and longevity. The importance of speed and power (think fast twitch muscle fiber) will be emphasized in this course since it is the least understood, and the least emphasized, BUT it is the modality that produces the best outcomes. The course will also cover, strength, mobility, flexibility, cardiovascular conditioning, and balance. Being able to get up and down on the floor on your own power is a prerequisite.

Develop your customized master layout and planting plan. Learn to create pleasing outdoor spatial relationships and plant selections that generate seasonal interest and visual curb-appeal. Begin with a site plan of your property drawn to scale and advance each week through the design, decision, and sketching process. Each session includes lecture, hands-on development, and planning time. Bring your property dimensions, building footprint, and current photos of environmental conditions.

Historical novels tell interesting stories about a time, a place, and the people living there. Authors must do extensive research so their writing accurately reflects the history. Using Horse by Geraldine Brooks as the launching point, this class will offer a one-hour look at the development of horse racing in America, with a focus on the social, economic, cultural, and racial impact of the horses themselves and the people around them. We will then spend an hour discussing the novel as contemporary literature. Readers and history buffs welcome! Participants should read "Horse" before class.

More than one hundred years after his death, Giacomo Puccini's operas continue to enthrall audiences. The gorgeous melodies and personal dramas of his operas make them just as potent today as they were a hundred years ago. Each week of this course will consist of an opening lecture followed by several audio and video examples that we will listen to and analyze in class. By the end of this course, students will have a deep familiarity with Puccini's "Four Big Operas" and an exposure to the most famous moments in his other works. These lectures will cover topics such as the composer's biography, the source material for the opera, the libretto/librettist, the composition, and famous performers and performances of each opera.

Halloween a religious observance? New Year's celebrated in March? The first Thanksgiving not in Massachusetts? Easter bunnies? Jack-O-Lanterns? Why are presidents elected on a Tuesday in November? Why is Labor Day not May 1? This class, the third in a series about the history of holidays, explores the origin and development of major American holidays and observances from New Year's to Easter and Halloween to Thanksgiving with numerous religious, patriotic, ethnic, commemorative, and celebratory stops along the way. (Christmas was covered in two previous classes.) As always, illustrations there will be aplenty.

Although many travelers use DSLR cameras, most topics in this course are pertinent to mobile devices. In this highly interactive course, you will learn about planning and logistics, basic gear and basic photography know-how, composition, storytelling, street photography, photographing local cultures, architecture, landscapes, iconic landmarks, and more!

To commemorate the 250 anniversary of the Declaration of Independence we will explore Abraham Lincoln's profound metaphor that described the Declaration of Independence as "the golden apple" and the Constitution as the "frame of silver" built to adorn and preserve it. This course will analyze the foundational principles of liberty and equality expressed in the Declaration's most famous passages. We will examine how the subsequent Constitution established the structure of government designed to implement and protect those ideals. Join us for four sessions to understand the essential, yet often complicated, relationship between these two indispensable documents in American history.

The Tony Awards are Broadway's biggest honor, celebrating the best in theater. Winning even one Tony is a huge achievement that comes from years of hard work. Winning multiple Tonys? That's something only the very best can do. In this class, we'll learn about the Broadway legends who have won the most Tony Awards. We'll meet amazing artists like director Bob Fosse (9 Tonys), producer Harold Prince (9), choreographer Gower Champion (8), actress Audra McDonald (6), and many others. We'll also look at the most award-winning shows in Broadway history, including Hello, Dolly! (14 Tonys), Cabaret (13), Hamilton (11), and A Chorus Line (9). Through videos and discussions, we'll discover what made these artists and shows so special. You'll learn what it takes to create Broadway magic at the highest level.

Shakespeare used the subject of free will constantly in his plays, poems, and narrative poems. At Shakespeare's time, major pronouncements about free will were emanating from learned minds and being exposed to the western world; and to Shakespeare. In this course we will examine Shakespeare's use of the matter of free will in six plays and coincidentally juxtapose the philosophical thoughts of six brilliant thinkers of his age on the same plays. The plays examined will be: Hamlet, Julius Caesar, King Lear, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet, and The Tempest. The six philosophers examined will be: Erasmus, Sir Thomas More, Martin Luther, Calvin, Montaigne, and Dante.

This is a hands on, step by step guide for learning Pointed Pen Calligraphy. We will use dip pens and ink. Information for further study will be provided. Learning from an instructor is preferable to trying to learn from books or in a situation where a teacher cannot guide you.

Get motivated by the grit of groundbreaking women! Join local author Sharon Spaulding in a lively discussion about trailblazing women whose accomplishments were dismissed, forgotten, or wrongly attributed. Spanning from Colonial America to the late 20th century, you'll be immersed in a kaleidoscope of backgrounds and experiences of women who stood for their beliefs. Be inspired by their courage and gain insight into how to forge your own path to accomplish your dream.

A "bildungsroman" is a coming-of-age novel, and this is one of my favorites. It explores what growing up means during a time of war--and what happens when the enemy is within. Knowles focuses on the war within the human heart, a personal war that leads inevitably to the loss of childhood innocence. The narrator fights his war at Devon, a private boys' boarding school, where he kills his enemy and makes "a separate peace."

Come play bridge with us! This is not a structured class, but a comfortable place to come and play with a teacher on hand in case you have questions. These bridge sessions were created with beginning bridge players in mind, but players of all skill levels are welcome, and we are happy to have you join us, with or without a partner.

This course is for anyone seeking knowledge about Alzheimer's disease, including those who are currently caregivers. The class is not suited for a person who is currently experiencing dementia. In addition to defining the seven clinical stages of Alzheimer's disease, the class will define and discuss the importance of person-centered care. The second session will include strategies, as well as hands-on demonstration of products, to support the physical and emotional needs of the person with dementia, as well as the caregiver.

Each week, Marcie's Movie Club will watch and then discuss a film at Salt Lake Film Society's Broadway Centre Cinemas-SLC's home for independent film. There will be a 1:45 introduction, 2:00 film, and a short discussion afterwards. Films will be recently released titles representing a variety of genres, including big-name, independent, documentary, and international titles. NOTE: Likely a majority of the films will be R-rated and may contain nudity, sexual situations, violence, and language that may trigger and/or offend some viewers. Films in 2025 included mainstream movies like ETERNITY and ONE BATTLE AFTER ANOTHER and also indie films like HAMNET and ELEANOR THE GREAT. We also saw documentaries like THE LIBRARIANS, as well as international films like SENTIMENTAL VALUE (Norway) and IT WAS JUST AN ACCIDENT (Iran), and the Oscar-nominated live-action and animated shorts. The class fee covers a movie ticket each week. If a class must be missed, club members will be offered complimentary tickets to watch the film or another one on their own at another time. Osher members will connect with one another over independent, first-run cinema, as well as with their fellow global citizens through documentary and international films. As Roger Ebert noted, movies are an empathy machine!

course_name: The Owl was a Baker's Daughter
description: Historical novels tell stories about a time and a place and the people who live there, requiring authors to do extensive research to reflect the history accurately. Using "The Owl was a Baker's Daughter" by Grace Tiffany as the focus, we will look at the 17th Century English Civil War, focusing on the conflict between Charles I's Royalists and Oliver Cromwell's Roundheads to provide context for the novel. We will then spend a second hour discussing the novel as literature. Readers and history buffs welcome! Please read "The Owl was a Baker's Daughter" before class.

course_name: Healthcare in the Age of AI
description: This course explores how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern healthcare and reshaping the patient experience. From predictive diagnostics and personalized medicine to virtual care and smart health technologies, we'll look at real innovations already making a difference--and those still on the horizon. Taught from a nursing perspective, the course also examines ethical considerations, data privacy, equity, and how to stay informed, confident, and empowered as AI becomes a larger part of everyday healthcare.
This course provides a structured forum where participants can explore the music, mythos, philosophy and concepts of love in Wagner's Tannhauser, Lohengrin, and Tristan und Isolde.

Just like Dorothy faced danger on the Yellow Brick Road, retirees also face threats to their financial well-being. Did you know that Utah leads the nation in fraud? Too many seniors have fallen victim and lost their life savings. And it is getting worse. In this class, become armed with the knowledge and street smarts needed to spot a scam before it drains your wallet.

This class will continue from where we left off in Ukulele for Beginners: Level One. You will continue to learn new songs, while expanding your knowledge of different types of strum patterns in different styles of music, such as folk, rock, blues, etc. There will be a deep dive into right hand finger picking and strumming techniques to make your songs sound more exciting and interesting. We learn three to four new songs that will allow you to apply the above techniques. You will also learn the basic fundamentals behind why it all works in a simple easy to understand manner. Finally, you can bring a song or two you may have been having trouble trying to learn on your own, and learn how to successfully troubleshoot any confusions or challenges with your newly acquired ukulele skills!

This short course will explore the various roles of museums as institutions of knowledge, preservation, and interpretation. The course will focus on the early history of museums in the United States and abroad, and provide a survey of topics such as exhibition practices, public education, visitor engagement, and building community relationships. Topics will be situated within the context of broader historical, intellectual, and cultural trends through time, and discussed from the instructor's personal experiences and perspectives working in archaeology and history museums.

This class is an introduction to qigong and simple stretching patterns. Movements will be taught both as physical and energetic exercises and as methods for improving present moment awareness and mindfulness of subtle perceptions. No special clothing or experience is required, come as you are, and be ready to move about comfortably in your home space and have fun with others! This course is offered in conjunction with several other Osher Institutes across the country. We will be meeting over Zoom, and the class will include social time with other class members. A signed liability waiver will be required prior to the first class. The instructor will offer supporting resources of a suggested DVD available for purchase, free videos to view on YouTube, and ongoing virtual classes between Osher terms.

Discover tips and tricks for using Google Maps. Create and save custom maps to share with friends and family. Learn to map your favorite restaurants, fishing holes, bike routes, golf courses, trail heads, etc. Explore the variety of features available in Google Maps through demos, hands-on activities, and discussion. Download off-line maps to use to navigate on mobile devices. Locate indoor maps and digital directories. Bring your laptop or tablet to class.

In a time of increasing division, the ability to engage in respectful, thoughtful conversations is more important than ever (even and especially with those you disagree with!). This six-week course introduces the Living Room Conversations model--an approach to discussing challenging topics in a controlled environment where all voices are heard and valued. Participants will learn how to practice active listening, curiosity, and bridge-building, learning how to navigate difficult discussions with empathy and understanding. Each week, we will cover specific skills and discuss a different topic together, fostering powerful connection and mutual learning. Weekly topics will include: Foundations of Civil Dialogue, Navigating Tricky Conversations, Finding Common Ground in Political Discussions, Communicating with Care and Empathy, Writing and Speaking for Impact, and Applying Civil Dialogue in Everyday Life.

This class is a bit hard to describe because it will be different every week!  Every time we meet, we'll look at important developments in science and technology that have come to light in the very recent past.  Because David is a biological scientist and Alan is a physical scientist, we could discuss anything from neutron stars to the bacteria in our intestines. The object is to help everyone understand 1) what happened, 2) why what happened is important, and 3) how the things that happened might affect our lives. No science background is necessary - just curiosity about what makes the world tick!

Have you ever wondered what a book is or why it came to be? Have you ever wondered why it looks the way it does, or what will happen to the book once we've all plugged into the digital world? Although we are comfortable with the idea and image of the book, defining "the book" is no easy task. In order to do so, we must trace the origins of its physical form, its readership and its content. Once we see where the book has been, we will be able to get a better idea of where the book is going.

Curious about artificial intelligence but not sure where to start? This interactive two-week class introduces you to AI tools like ChatGPT and beyond, showing you how they can be useful, entertaining, and even surprising. We'll discuss practical applications, creative uses, and ethical considerations, all in a fun and accessible way. NOTE: the title and description for this class were created by ChatGPT! It even helped me write my biography.

The classical music composers of the last several centuries have written memorable compositions that we hear today in many symphony concert halls. The more contemporary composers of today either write contemporary classical music or in many cases find themselves writing film score music for the movies. Many of the film score composers are European and have made a very big name for themselves in this art form. Hollywood realized many years ago just how important a facit music is to motion pictures.  Music creates a mood, not to mention a complete backdrop to what is going on. This course addresses the history of music in the movies and the wonderful composers who have enriched our viewing experience.

This single-session lecture explores the Declaration of Independence as a revolutionary statement of political ideals, defining America not just as a place, but as a bold ideology rooted in liberty, equality, and the belief in self-government for all people.

This is the first of five courses on political theory, which cover a spectrum of political ideologies (defined as organized systems of beliefs and values). The goal is to genuinely understand both sides of the Left/Right political spectrum, and to identify and clarify your own political worldview. We start in this course with Traditional Conservatism, which is the most difficult political ideology to explain and clarify. First the origin of American political order in the form of the liberal state--represented by the US Constitution--is explained. Then the Right/Left political spectrum is identified and defined in terms of political ideologies. This is followed by discussion of the works of four conservative political philosophers: Michael Freeden, Yorum Hazony, Thomas Sowell, and Russell Kirk. The entire future series of five courses will include Parts: (1) Traditional Conservatism, (2) Conservatism and Libertarianism, (3) Liberalism, (4) Moral and Cultural Foundations of the American Political Divide, and (5) AI and Political Theory.

Do your joints ache when you move? Do you want to have more energy? Join us for a gentle exercise class designed for anyone who wants to feel and move better, even if you do not have arthritis. This class offers a gentle warm-up for the joints, followed by movement to enhance balance, coordination, strength as well as cardiovascular fitness. Class will always conclude with a gentle cooldown and relaxation session. The class is open to all levels of fitness. Attendees can be seated or standing to participate in the sessions.

Hippocrates wrote, "Wherever the art of medicine is loved, there is also a love of humanity." Literature is an art that best describes illness, the people who are affected by it, and the people who treat it. We will read and discuss essays, short stories, and poems, written by doctors, patients, and by brilliant authors that may include: Sir William Osler, William Carlos Williams, Mikhail Bulgalov, Jorge Luis Borges, Pablo Neruda, WH Auden, Eudora Welty, May Sarton, Lewis Thomas, Anatole Broyard, Denise Levertov, Richard Selzer, John Stone, Raymond Carver, and Perri Klass.

Fidelio is a stirring saga of love, bravery, and the quest for justice. In this heroic tale, Leonore goes undercover, disguised as a guard named Fidelio, to infiltrate a corrupt prison and rescue her wrongfully accused husband, Florestan. It's an emotional journey that reflects Beethoven's idealism, echoing his own conviction that good will triumphs over tyranny. With the hopeful "Prisoners' Chorus" and soaring overture, Fidelio is a testament to Beethoven's musical genius--be the first to experience this brand-new production, incorporating modernized dialogue and thought-provoking projections that underscore the power of the human spirit. Utah Opera's preview class will provide insights into the story and the music, as well as the production history of Beethoven's only opera, "Fidelio." We will also present fascinating information about Utah Opera's production and its cast. Interested class members can linger after the hour-long class session to observe a rehearsal on-site.

Examine current political and governmental issues breaking that day and week--locally, nationally, and internationally! This class is highly interactive. Controversial questions are scrutinized. Group discussions are encouraged. Readings from The New York Times and NPR, as well as local newspapers and Internet sources, will be provided. News articles and videos seed the discussion, but often grow into entirely different topics based on student interest and participation. Students are encouraged to ask hard questions, and to participate actively and respectfully in class discussion.

This transformative class explores the profound art of connecting with horses through presence, breath, and mutual understanding. Far beyond traditional horsemanship, this experience invites participants to develop a deep, intuitive relationship with these magnificent beings without the barrier of riding. Class members will each be interacting and connecting with horses (not riding them).
